articles.title: Sabalenka edges Noskova, keeps US Open treble bid alive
articles.summary: Two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka rallied in the final set to beat Linda Noskova on Tuesday and reach a sixth straight US Open semi-final.Tiafoe do...
articles.body:
Two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka rallied in the final set to beat Linda Noskova on Tuesday and reach a sixth straight US Open semi-final.

Sabalenka triumphed 7-6 (7/1), 3-6, 7-6 (10/7) over the 21-year-old Wimbledon champion, who went toe to toe with the world number one on Arthur Ashe Stadium -- where men's defending champion Carlos Alcaraz faced eighth-seeded American Ben Shelton in the last match of the night.

"What a battle," Sabalenka told the crowd. "I was pushing myself to the limit, especially in the third set.

"I honestly thought that was it, the match was over, and that's what helped me to feel loose and go for my shots," added the Belarusian star, who trailed 4-2 in the third set having surrendered a break in a fifth game featuring two double faults.

Sabalenka looked headed for another Grand Slam disappointment in a season in which she has so far been unable to add to her stash of four major titles.

Clearly frustrated, she nevertheless regrouped and broke Noskova to love to pull level at 4-4.

They hurtled to the 10-point tiebreaker -- where Sabalenka dropped the first two points before climbing back and finally sealing victory with a courageous second-serve ace.

Noskova fired 18 aces -- 46 winners in all to Sabalenka's 42 -- as she became the first player to take a set off Sabalenka in the tournament.

Sabalenka has now won 18 straight matches at Flushing Meadows, and she must keep going to a third straight title if she is to have any chance to retain the world number one ranking she has held since October of 2024.

Even the title might not do it. Second-ranked Elena Rybakina can grab the top spot if she beats Zheng Qinwen in their quarter-final on Wednesday.

The victory was Sabalenka's first win over a top-10 player since she beat Coco Gauff in the Miami final in March.

That was her third title of 2026, but Sabalenka has struggled since, exiting early at both Roland Garros and Wimbledon.

The Belarusian will next face the winner of the all-American quarter-final between third seed Jessica Pegula and Emma Navarro.

A two-time winner on the WTA tour this year, 2024 finalist Pegula took a 4-0 record over Navarro into their last-eight clash.

American 11th seed Frances Tiafoe also had to go the distance, rallying from two sets down and erasing a 3-0 deficit in the fifth set to beat 22-year-old compatriot Alex Michelsen 5-7, 3-6, 7-5, 6-3, 7-6 (10/6).

Michelsen, ranked 46th, had reached his first Grand Slam quarter-final without dropping a set. He served for the match at 5-4 in the third.

"He gave me some gifts, a couple of double faults there," Tiafoe said. "But then I slowly started to get my rhythm there, snuck out third set and slowly started playing better and better.

"But he is a hell of a player," Tiafoe added of Michelsen, who wept in Tiafoe's arms as they met at the net after four hours and 38 minutes. "He should have easily won today."

Tiafoe dominated the fourth set, and when Michelsen responded Tiafoe refused to fold, battling back to force the decider and reaching the semi-finals in Flushing Meadows for the third time in five years.

He will face either Alcaraz or Shelton in the semi-finals.

Alcaraz faces his toughest test of the tournament in Shelton, who said he expects the Spaniard to be at full strength despite the fact that the seven-time Grand Slam champion is playing his first tournament in more than four months after recovering from a right wrist injury.

articles.title: SEC files amendment for authority to expel LSU from league, cites Kiffin’s Clemson halftime comments
articles.summary: The SEC’s presidents and chancellors will meet Thursday.
articles.body:
The SEC filed an amendment to its federal lawsuit against LSU, Lane Kiffin and school officials on Tuesday.

The league seeks the authority to expel LSU from the conference.

"The SEC and its member universities have the right to establish, through agreed-upon governance procedures, the rules under which they voluntarily compete and to expect those rules to be followed," the SEC said in a statement. "A commitment to those rules, and to the core principles of the Southeastern Conference, is an essential element of SEC membership.

"Today's filing is necessary to defend that right and preserve the Conference's ability to govern competition among its members."

The SEC, per Pete Thamel , is not expected to expel LSU from the league. However, the the filing does indicate, per the report, "the seriousness of the league as it attempts to affirm the legal right to enforce its own rules."

The SEC's presidents and chancellors will meet Thursday to decide whether to terminate LSU as an SEC member institution pursuant to Section 3.1.5 of the SEC Constitution and Bylaws, which give the presidents the "plenary power and authority with respect to all affairs of the Conference of any type or nature whatsoever," including the power to "(t)ake all actions specified and contemplated in Article 3 (of the Constitution) in their sole discretion."

Under SEC rules, a vote of at least two-thirds of all the presidents is required to terminate a school's membership.

Interestingly enought, the SEC's amended complaint made note that during halftime of No. 10 LSU's 51-10 victory against Clemson on Saturday, Kiffin told Holly Rowe "imagine if we had pro players," which, of course, was a reference to Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris, who had signed NFL contracts before attempting to return to school.

The SEC alleges that Kiffin's statements "stand in sharp contrast to the silence by the President and Athletic Director of LSU" and "they confirm the lack of institutional control over the athletics program at LSU that is required by Article 6 of the SEC Constitution and by the remaining provisions of the Constitution and Bylaws."

Last Thursday, the SEC filed a federal lawsuit in the Northern District of Alabama that listed LSU, new president Wade Rouse, athletic director Verge Ausberry and Kiffin, among others, as defendants.

The federal complaint comes down to a First Amendment claim against LSU for pursuing and attempting to roster former professional athletes because it infringes on the conference's ability to properly serve its other members and enforce its own rules against such conduct.

articles.title: Caleb Williams, Ben Johnson, Chicago Bears about to take fans on a fun ride
articles.summary: The incoherent ramblings of a belligerent Bears fan. Bill Zimmerman dives into why this is the most exciting time to be a Bears fan since 1986.
articles.body:
I was writing some articles after the 53-man roster was announced and discussing how I have several concerns about the Chicago Bears defense, mostly the defensive line.

A handful of fans on social media and in the comments section decided to voice their opinions that I am too negative. And truth be told, I probably am. Being a Bears fan with this much failure over the last 35 years will do that to a person.

But I am excited about the future here with Ben Johnson, and certainly excited about the future of Caleb Williams .

But my negativity doesn't reflect them or the offense in any way. My negativity is about trying to win a Super Bowl and the moves the Bears made (or mostly did not make) that make me think that goal is still out of reach in 2026. That's what frustrates me.

But with the dawn of a new season upon us, let's not focus on the negatives; I'm sure I will have plenty of columns that voice my frustrations at one point or another. But let's focus on the positives about where this team is, and where it's going.

Because if we are being honest, this should be the most excited you have been for a team entering a season since September of 1986.

That's right. This is the most exciting start to a season since 1986. This is better than 2019. This is better than 2007. In both 2007 and 2019, the Bears were coming off great seasons, but there were quarterback problems.

Even when you look at the coaches. Matt Nagy did fairly well here. Obviously, Lovie Smith did very well here. But with either of those two coaches, were you ever 100% certain the Bears had an elite coach? A good coach? I'm sure many did, but did you ever think either of those coaches was one of the top three in the league?

This is a totally different world. The Bears have, at minimum, a top-10 coach in the league; many experts would already put Ben Johnson in the top 5. And guess what? He's pretty new at this, and he's only getting better.

I've been on the Caleb Williams bandwagon since the beginning (the beginning being the horrible start to the 2023 season). Perhaps it's my jaded views of Chicago Bears quarterbacks, but I had him approaching the top 10 QBs in the league after last season, but when you look around the league, he's almost at a consensus of already being in the top 10.

How far can Caleb Williams fly this year? If everything goes the way Ben Johnson sees it, Williams is going to be in the top 5. He's going to be in the same breath as Mahomes , Allen, Jackson, Stafford , and Burrow. He's going to start becoming a regular conversation as part of the MVP race every season.

Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams have changed the entire dynamic of the Chicago Bears franchise, and it's incredibly awesome that we've arrived.

Because of those two, the Chicago Bears will always have a place at the table. How many teams do you consider to have a top-10 QB and a top-10 coach in the NFL? Let's take a look.

Andy Reid and Patrick Mahomes are one. Josh Allen and Lamar Jackson have new coaches. Joe Burrow has Zac Taylor, and Taylor is not at that level. Matthew Stafford and Sean McVay are two. I think you need to put Justin Herbert and Jim Harbaugh there. That's three. You can't put Schottenheimer there with Dak Prescott . You could make the argument that Drake Maye and Mike Vrabel are both there. That's four. And then there's Caleb and Ben. That's five.

What does that group of 5 have in common? Harbaugh and Herbert have been to the playoffs both years together. Maye and Vrabel made it in their only year; same with Caleb and Ben. McVay and Stafford have made it 4 of 5 years, and the one year they missed, Stafford missed 8 games.

Mahomes and Reid made it 7 consecutive years and won three of five Super Bowl appearances.

What am I trying to say? When you have a great coach and a great QB, you make the playoffs almost every year.

That's what the Chicago Bears are entering.

Now, the roster may still need some TLC to get it to a point where it's truly contending for a Super Bowl, but the Chicago Bears are entering a time where they should be a perennial playoff team every year.

The Chicago Bears finally have a place at the table.

Not only will the Bears be competing for playoff spots every year, but they are going to have the most explosive offense any living fan has ever seen. This offense is only getting better. Luther Burden and Colston Loveland are about to become elite weapons. Rome Odunze and D'Andre Swift have established themselves. Ben Johnson won't let the offensive line be bad. Ever.

This offense is going to be elite every year with the coach and QB combo.

It's going to be like something we've never experienced.

NFL experts are going to do film studies on this offense. Ben Johnson's coaching tree will become a thing like Sean McVay's has.

Nine times in Bears history has a QB thrown for over 3,000 yards and 20 TDs. Caleb Williams owns two of those in two seasons. He's going to rewrite the Chicago Bears passing records.

Ben Johnson is going to rewrite the Chicago Bears' records for offense. Heck, Ben Johnson may become one of the top 10 most winning coaches in the history of the franchise THIS season.

It's a golden time to be a Chicago Bears fan. We are entering an era that we've never experienced. This is going to be new to all of us. But it's going to be really f'ing fun.

So buckle up, Bears fans. The Chicago Bears are no longer an NFL doormat. They are going to consistently be one of the better teams in the league.

This is what Bears fans have wanted since Mike Ditka was carried off the field at the Louisiana Superdome, and it's hard to imagine that the dream has become a reality.

Enjoy it. Not just last season. Not just this season. But every season. Enjoy it. Enjoy all of it. Embrace the greatness we are about to witness year in and year out.

The Chicago Bears have arrived. Bears fans are excited. TV Networks are excited. Roger Goodell is excited.

As Jerry Seinfeld once said, "That's a shame."

Embrace it all. I have. What a time to be alive.

articles.title: Michigan Fans Split On Bryce Underwood Ahead Of Oklahoma
articles.summary: Michigan fans are split on Bryce Underwood after the Western Michigan escape, with Oklahoma next. #GoBlue
articles.body:
The Michigan Wolverines are 1-0 entering Week 2 of the college football season, and so are the Oklahoma Sooners . The two meet at Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor with kickoff set for noon ET Saturday on FOX , and Michigan fans are nowhere near agreement on what Bryce Underwood is about to do in it.

Even with the Wolverines looking toward Week 2, many college football fans are still in disbelief about Michigan beating the Western Michigan Broncos 13-12 in the opener. Underwood's 47-yard touchdown pass to JJ Buchanan came on an untimed final play, after officials reviewed the clock and put a second back on it . Many fans believe Michigan should be 0-1. It is not.

Oklahoma is carrying no such doubt into the weekend. The Sooners opened with a 51-0 win over UTEP on Sept. 4 behind quarterback John Mateer.

Bryce Underwood Has To Be Better Against Oklahoma

As Week 2 approaches, the Wolverines have to show a lot of improvement against the Sooners. The biggest one is the quarterback play of Bryce Underwood. If he does not play well, Michigan has a backup ready: head coach Kyle Whittingham named true freshman Tommy Carr the No. 2 quarterback before the season, ahead of Colorado State transfer Brayden Fowler-Nicolosi.

Michigan Fans Are Split On Bryce Underwood

Some Michigan fans are looking forward to seeing what could happen in Week 2 against Oklahoma. Others are already bracing for it. This is what some of the Wolverines fans said on X.

That is the confident wing of the fan base. This is the other one.

A day after the Western Michigan game, some fans skipped the debate entirely and went to the depth chart.

It will be interesting to see whether Underwood struggles again against the Sooners. If that happens, would Whittingham put Carr in at quarterback? That is something that remains to be seen. The whole college football world will be watching the Sooners and the Wolverines on Saturday.

articles.title: Which uniforms are Rams and 49ers wearing in Week 1?

articles.body:
It's almost time for the Los Angeles Rams to kick off their 2026 season. They'll do so on Thursday night against the San Francisco 49ers in what's technically a home game … 8,000 miles from SoFi Stadium.

The Rams are "hosting" the 49ers in Melbourne, Australia, the first NFL game ever played on the continent. It's a marquee matchup between two bitter rivals, which is the perfect way for these teams to get the new season started.

After wearing white jerseys all preseason, the Rams will go with a classic look for the regular-season opener. They're wearing their royal blue jerseys and yellow pants on Thursday night, an iconic combination for this storied franchise.

The 49ers will contrast the Rams' colored jerseys by wearing white uniforms on the road. They'll be in their white primaries to start the year, not their all-white throwbacks, so they'll pair those tops with gold pants.

Kickoff on Thursday night is set for 8:35 p.m. ET, which will be 10:35 a.m. Australia time on Friday morning.

articles.body:
Bismack Biyombo was one of the few players to suit up for both the Charlotte Bobcats and the Charlotte Hornets , as his tenure with the franchise overlapped with the team's name change. Biyombo, who wore the No. 0, was acquired on a draft night trade in 2011 after being selected with the No. 7 overall pick by the Sacramento Kings . Biyombo spent four seasons with Charlotte before signing a free agent deal with the Toronto Raptors ahead of the 2015-16 season. The Congolese native would return to the franchise later on in his career for three more seasons but would wear a different number (No. 8).

During those four seasons to begin his career, Biyombo averaged 4.4 points, 6.4 rebounds, 0.3 assists, 0.3 steals and 1.6 blocks. Now a 15-year NBA veteran, Biyombo most recently played for the San Antonio Spurs , who finished runner-up to the New York Knicks during the 2025-26 season. articles.title: Houston Astros' Christian Vázquez defies the odds to catch 1,000 MLB games
articles.summary: Christian Vázquez jokes about going bald, but his path to 1,000 games caught shows why pitchers and winning teams have trusted him for years.
articles.body:
PHILADELPHIA - Of the three active players who have appeared in at least 1,000 games at catcher in the majors, two were on the field Tuesday night at Citizens Bank Park.

J.T. Realmuto of the Phillies is well beyond that number, catching his 1,386th career game Tuesday, which ranks 47th all-time, per Baseball Reference. Christian Vázquez , the Houston Astros veteran, reached it on Saturday, becoming the 129th catcher to appear in 1,000 games behind the plate in MLB.

"I never thought I was going to catch 1,000 games in my career in the big leagues, so it's special," said Vázquez. "A lot of innings behind the plate. That's why I'm bald - thinking too much."

The subtle manner in which Vázquez reached 1,000 games caught, entering as a defensive replacement, befit his road there. Vázquez has played 100-plus games in only four of his 12 major-league seasons. He entered Tuesday with a career 78 OPS-plus; a 100 OPS-plus is league average.

Behind the plate, Vázquez has accrued positive defensive runs saved in all but one season, however, per Sports Info Solutions. The 36-year-old has played for two World Series champions, caught an additional 30 games in the postseason and accrued a dozen years of MLB service time.

"You have to be able to be really smart, putting the right fingers down, (and) health is huge for someone to be able to do that," Astros manager Joe Espada said. "He's done it on winning teams, too, he's won World Series, so that tells you how good he is and how valuable he is to winning teams."

The Astros signed Vázquez to a minor-league contract late this spring and carried him as their backup to Yainer Diaz . Due to Diaz's oblique strain in the first half, Vázquez leads the team in innings caught, albeit also with a notable record. The Astros entered Tuesday with a 43-28 record with Vázquez in the starting lineup this season and a 30-45 mark when he was not.

Vázquez's defensive metrics have remained positive this season. Sports Info Solutions assessed him five runs saved at catcher entering Tuesday. Statcast ranked Vázquez tied for fifth out of 59 qualified catchers with plus-six framing runs, albeit with below-average marks in blocking and throwing. Vázquez owned a 22.2% caught-stealing rate; league rate was 23%.

After Vázquez, the closest active catchers to 1,000 games caught entering Tuesday were James McCann (940), Travis d'Arnaud (879) and Austin Hedges (856).

"When I signed (with the Red Sox from Puerto Rico), I was like a fourth catcher in rookie ball," Vázquez said. "So now, seeing where I landed in my career is amazing. They gave me an opportunity and it was history after that."

Vázquez caught the second World Series no-hitter in MLB history in 2022 with the Astros, receiving their combined no-hitter in Game 4 against the Phillies. He also won a World Series title in 2018 with Boston . The Astros are attempting a return to this year's postseason, entering Tuesday with a two-game lead on the Rangers in the American League West and 18 games left on their regular-season schedule.

"I think when teams or people see that you care about your pitchers, your team, you love to win, I think they love that," Vázquez said. "I think nothing's better than in October having the trophy in my hands."

articles.title: ‘Almost as sad as the millions he stole’: Concern and disgust mount as Brett Favre appears to be worsening rapidly
articles.summary: In 2024, Hall of Fame quarterback Brett Favre revealed that he is battling Parkinson’s disease, a degenerative nervous system disorder that causes parts of t...
articles.body:
In 2024, Hall of Fame quarterback Brett Favre revealed that he is battling Parkinson's disease, a degenerative nervous system disorder that causes parts of the brain to deteriorate and motor functions to decline.

"Sadly, I also lost an investment in a company that I believed was developing a breakthrough concussion drug I thought would help others," Favre said about Prevacus, a company making a concussion drug that received $2 million of Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) funds.

"And I'm sure you'll understand why it's too late for me, because I've recently been diagnosed with Parkinson's. This is also a cause dear to my heart."

More recently, the former Super Bowl champion and Green Bay Packers legend shared a video shouting out Colectivo Packers Mexico, and it was clear how much tough his battle with the disease has been, as he struggles to speak clearly.

Concern for Favre mounted from his fans on social media, although many couldn't look past the situation involving Prevacus.

"So sad to see. Almost as sad as the millions he stole from families dependent on welfare," one fan posted on X.

"As a little boy, he was my favorite QB. As a grown man, I've been extremely disappointed in his shady actions and downright racist commentary. However, I still appreciate the old days and wish the guy well," someone else added.

"One of the all time greats and it looks like a the game has had an affect on his brain health," another fan added.

Hopefully, both the affected families in Mississippi and Favre receive all of the help and assistance that they need. As of the time of this writing, he has repaid the $1.1 million principal for speeches he never gave, but still owes the state $730,000 in interest.

articles.title: Running back rooms in the spotlight ahead of Patriots vs. Seahawks season opener
articles.summary: Comparing the two position groups ahead of Week 1.
articles.body:
The New England Patriots and the Seattle Seahawks have seen changes to their offensive backfields in the offseason. The more drastic shift overall was Seattle's, but the Patriots also have a situation with their second-year back that shouldn't be ignored.

The Seahawks are entering the year coming off a dominating Super Bowl win against the Patriots, in which Kenneth Walker III, the fourth-year rusher who started every game in 2025, was awarded Super Bowl MVP. Walker carried the ball 27 times, and picked up 135 yards on the ground. He also hauled in two receptions for 26 yards in the championship game.

Last season, Walker rushed for 1,027 yards, which was the first time he had for over 1,000 yards since his rookie year back in 2022. After his eye-popping performance in the 29-13 win over the Patriots, the star back hit free agency. Walker ended up landing with the Kansas City Chiefs on a three-year deal, worth up to $45 million.

So, where does this leave the Seahawks now? They answered that question 45 days later on Day 1 of the NFL Draft, when they used the last pick of the first round to acquire Jadarian Price. Price was a four-star recruit out of high school, and became a member of the Fighting Irish in 2022. But after suffering a season-ending ruptured achilles tendon in the offseason of what would have been his true freshman year, he began his college football career in 2023. Throughout his college tenure, he racked up 1,692 yards, and found the end zone 21 times on the ground.

Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel praised Jadarian Price when asked about him.

"Jadarian's got great speed," Vrabel said. "He's a slasher. He'll test edges. He's got great patience. But, I watched him circle guys up in college fairly easily. So, the speed, I think, is real."

Price will now be the feature running back for the reigning champs in his rookie campaign, although this likely wouldn't have been the case if it weren't for an injury to Zach Charbonnet .

Charbonnet tore his ACL in the 41-6 rout of the San Francisco 49ers in last year's divisional round of the playoffs. The 25-year-old is coming off of a career high in carries and rushing yards, and he was also tied for sixth in all of the NFL with 12 touchdowns. All of which came in a secondary role behind Walker. So while Charbonnet looked as if this would have been his first year as the primary back, it will have to wait as the Seahawks look at what they have with Price. Entering Wednesday, it will be George Holani and Emanuel Wilson behind the first-round pick.

As for the Patriots, the halfback room will look mostly the same. Rhamondre Stevenson is expected to take possession of the RB1 role, with Treveyon Henderson behind him. Stevenson, entering his sixth season with the Patriots, had his lead role pressured the most last season since Ezekiel Elliott back in 2023: Henderson ended up recording 911 rushing yards to Stevenson's 603, and scoring nine touchdowns to seven for Stevenson. However, Stevenson provided a little bit more of steady option in backfield compared to Henderson, who's numbers were inflated by long, explosive runs.

Vrabel expressed that the running back room has a variety of skills sets, explaining that, "some guys have a little bit of different strengths than maybe the other guys. So, there's a little bit of everything."

However, Henderson has now been ruled out for Week 1 with an ankle injury . The 2025 second-round draft pick has been dealing with this injury since aggravating it during practice on August 24.

A trade that could become increasingly important

With Henderson unavailable, Corey Kiner , the Patriots' trade acquisition from the Arizona Cardinals , projects to play an elevated role. Kiner, like Henderson, is heading into his sophomore season in the NFL.

An undrafted free agent signing by the 49ers, he suffered a high ankle sprain in his rookie preseason that led to his release. He then was signed to the Minnesota Vikings practice squad, and never touched the field while he was there. Lastly, Kiner was picked up by the Cardinals off the Vikings' practice squad, which is where he appeared in his first professional game.

While he only carried the ball 12 times for 58 yards last year, Vrabel and the Patriots saw something in him.

"He was a player that we had looked at trying to get last year coming out," conveyed Vrabel. "He's a good young runner."

The hype around the Patriots versus Seahawks rematch is real, which was defined by the running game in the Super Bowl. The Patriots will look to match the production the Seahawks got out of that position last year, and kickoff the new season with a huge win in Seattle — but doing so without the big-play threat that is Henderson could prove to be a challenge.

articles.title: Tiafoe gives Michelsen a hug and a shoulder to cry on after his US Open victory
articles.summary: Frances Tiafoe knew Alex Michelsen needed a shoulder to cry on.  Michelsen was playing in his first Grand Slam quarterfinal and was just a few points from wi...
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — Frances Tiafoe knew Alex Michelsen needed a shoulder to cry on.

So after handing his fellow American a crushing defeat in the U.S. Open quarterfinals Tuesday, Tiafoe held Michelsen in a long embrace while the 22-year-old sobbed into his shoulder .

Michelsen was playing in his first Grand Slam quarterfinal and was just a few points from winning it after taking the first two sets. The No. 11-seeded Tiafoe came back to win 5-7, 3-6, 7-5, 6-3, 7-6 (10-6), starting his turnaround after Michelsen failed to serve out the match with a 5-4 lead in the third set.

"But he's a hell of a player, man," Tiafoe said. "I mean, he easily could have won today so shout out to Alex Michelsen."

This was the third pro match between the two, with Tiafoe winning both previous encounters. Michelsen said after his fourth-round victory that he had improved and would try to change things.

"He's also an unbelievable guy and a very good friend of mine," Michelsen added.

Tiafoe is 28, one of the leaders of American men's tennis and a fan favorite at the U.S. Open, where he has reached his third semifinal.

He said Sunday in looking ahead to the match that he had developed a friendship with Michelsen.

"We have a good relationship," he said. "We're always laughing and joking."

Michelsen left the court with a towel on his head, raising his arm to acknowledge the cheers from the crowd.

articles.title: Paul Finebaum explains how USC head coach Lincoln Riley’s hot seat can cool down
articles.summary: Lincoln Riley's seat may be getting warm at USC, but Paul Finebaum believes the Trojans head coach has a chance to cool things down with Jayden Maiava leadin...
articles.body:
The college football season is underway, and there's a lot of pressure on head coaches. Not only are several coaches taking over new programs with expectations to deliver, but some are also entering the season with their jobs on the line.

For USC Trojans head coach Lincoln Riley, he's not quite on his last leg. However, there's no doubt his seat has been getting warm. Despite this, one analyst thinks there's a good chance it could cool down.

Paul Finebaum discussed coaches who could get off the hot seat this year, and Riley was one of the biggest names he mentioned. The key? Quarterback Jayden Maiava .

"I would say Lincoln Riley's got a chance this year. He's got a great quarterback. He still can never seem to win a big game." Finebaum said on his Paul Finebaum Show.

Nov 29, 2025; Los Angeles, California, USA; Southern California Trojans quarterback Jayden Maiava (14) and head coach Lincoln Riley react after the game against the UCLA Bruins at United Airlines Field at Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

There's one major aspect that stands out for Riley that few coaches can match: his ability to recruit and develop quarterbacks. Riley has helped multiple quarterbacks reach the NFL, including Baker Mayfield , Kyler Murray , and Caleb Williams , who was selected first overall.

Despite this, USC has posted just a 37-18 record with no College Football Playoff appearances under Riley. When he was Oklahoma 's head coach, he led the Sooners to three playoff appearances.

Making the jump from Oklahoma to USC came with massive expectations. USC, after all, has significantly greater resources to recruit with in the modern NIL era.

Maiava could be Riley's game changer. He's more than capable of making big plays for USC, and he could hear his name called early in April's NFL Draft.

Sep 4, 2026; Los Angeles, California, USA; Southern California Trojans quarterback Jayden Maiava (14) throws the ball before the game against the Fresno State Bulldogs at United Airlines Field at Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

Riley recruited Maiava through the transfer portal from UNLV . Maiava has improved his game each year and is off to a hot start in 2026. Could he help Riley and USC finally break through and reach the College Football Playoff?

USC's place in the Big Ten makes that challenge even more difficult. The Trojans will have to contend with powerhouse programs such as Ohio State, Oregon , and Indiana. The biggest question for Riley's team is whether its defense can make enough plays to at least become an average unit.

If it can, and Maiava continues on his current trajectory, it could be a big year for both the USC Trojans and Riley.

articles.title: Tiafoe consoles tearful Michelsen after remarkable comeback
articles.summary: Frances Tiafoe comes from two sets and a break down to beat Alex Michelsen in a thrilling comeback to reach the US Open semi-finals.
articles.body:
Frances Tiafoe came from two sets and a break down to beat Alex Michelsen in a thrilling comeback to reach the US Open semi-finals.

American 11th seed Tiafoe was outplayed by world number 46 Michelsen for the first half of the match, but battled back from 5-3 down in the third set - with his opponent serving for the match - to ignite a remarkable turnaround.

In a final set of multiple breaks and swings of momentum, Tiafoe triumphed in the 10-point tie-break to win 5-7 3-6 7-5 6-3 7-6 (10-6).

Victory means 28-year-old Tiafoe reaches his third US Open semi-final in five years, where he will play defending champion Carlos Alcaraz or American eighth seed Ben Shelton.

Michelsen, 22, who was competing in his first Grand Slam quarter-final, was in tears as the pair embraced after a match which lasted four hours and 38 minutes.

"In the end I slowly started to get my rhythm. Snuck out that third set and got better and better," said Tiafoe.

"He's a hell of a player and he easily could have won today. Shout out to Alex Michelsen.

"Everyone was asleep in the first couple of hours, I was too. As it went along the energy was incredible as it is always. You guys are rooting for me and I appreciate that."

Unseeded Michelsen came into the match in fine form, having not dropped a set at the tournament prior to facing Tiafoe, and grasped the momentum in the first set.

After the pair traded breaks of serve early in the match, Michelsen got the deciding break at 6-5 in a set where he fired 15 winners to Tiafoe's four.

Michelsen continued to have the upper hand, with his backhand proving decisive on key points and, after taking the second set, he went up a break early in the third.

It was not until Michelsen was serving for the match at 5-4 that nerves began to hit. He served two double faults and Tiafoe broke to level, won the set and took the opening three games of the fourth set.

After holding Michelsen off, Tiafoe took the match to a deciding set where the pair traded multiple breaks of serve - invigorating the spectators on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

A fan favourite, Tiafoe thrived off the energy of the New York crowd as he then got the better of the tie-break to seal his fourth five-set victory at a major in 2026.

Tiafoe is hoping to reach the final at Flushing Meadows for the first time, following defeats by Alcaraz in 2022 and Taylor Fritz in 2024.

articles.title: Steelers made contract offer to CB Joey Porter Jr.
articles.summary: Pittsburgh’s offer to the star corner remains ‘not good enough,’ NFL Network’s Mike Garafolo reported.
articles.body:
The Steelers have made a contract offer to cornerback Joey Porter Jr. , NFL Network's Mike Garafolo reported late Tuesday. However, the insider noted the proposed deal was "not good enough for this one to be deemed close."

"But, the Steelers have shown a willingness to engage," Garafolo added. "Which means we got a couple of days for both sides to figure out what are the right numbers to get a deal done. There is a lot of work to be done from my understanding. I would not call it imminent. I would not call it close. But I will call it an actual negotiation now that the Steelers have made an offer."

Porter is now the last big-name cornerback still hoping for an extension this offseason, with the Patriots and cornerback Christian Gonzalez agreeing to a record-setting four-year, $135 million deal early Tuesday morning.

With Porter back in practice after spending most of the summer on the physically unable to perform list, it appears the two sides are starting to make some progress. However, Pittsburgh doesn't negotiate once games start, and Porter hasn't ruled out an in-season holdout, adding an extra sense of urgency to the negotiations.

Steelers beat writers such as PennLive's Nick Farabaugh have posted that the Steelers will probably not need to make Porter the league's new highest-paid corner to get a deal done.

articles.title: LA Times sports editor says that college football schedules need to change due to 'climate change'
articles.summary: Texas Longhorns fans fled to the concourse seeking shade as extreme heat sparked debate over college football scheduling in early September.
articles.body: Out of the many storylines surrounding the first week and a half of college football season, one of the most unexpected was, of all things, weather. It started when the USC Trojans hosted San Jose State in Week 0 at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum in front of a sparse crowd. The LA area was beset by an unusually hot and humid spell of weather, thanks to remnants of a tropical storm off the West Coast. Combined with a brutal noon start time that provided no shade or relief throughout the game, the conditions meant there weren’t many fans brave enough, or quite frankly dumb enough, to endure a heat index of roughly 105 degrees. For a game that was decided within minutes of kickoff. That continued into Week 1, with teams like South Carolina and the Texas Longhorns hosting games during the middle of the afternoon sun in extreme heat. While more fans bought tickets, or even showed up to the stadium, many smartly left as soon as possible. Or in Texas' case, huddled under the concourse in hopes of finding shade. Some had to be treated for medical conditions like heat exhaustion or dehydration. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! This has sparked debate over the wisdom of scheduling games in the middle of the afternoon, in August or early September, in hotter climates. Justifiably so. But it also gave rise to one of the more ridiculous contentions you'll ever see, and a near-perfect example of the decline of sportswriting as a profession and the reputation of the Los Angeles Times: blaming it on climate change. In response to a post describing and photographing a large group of Longhorns fans trying to escape the heat at DKR, LA Times assistant managing editor and sports editor Iliana Limon Romero said that programs should change scheduling to "adapt to climate change." DOES USC'S POOR OPENING GAME ATTENDANCE MEAN LINCOLN RILEY'S ON THE HOT SEAT ALREADY? "At some point, schools and TV networks are going to have to adapt to climate change and stop expecting fans to tolerate extreme heat as a badge of honor supporting their teams," she posted on X. Oh boy. Several things can be true at once. TV networks ignoring the reality of local conditions at noon or mid-afternoon in late summer in Texas or South Carolina because it fits their preferred broadcast window is a real concern. There's no reason games in Austin in the first week of September should be played anytime other than at night. It's also true that the symbolic "badge of honor" fans get from subjecting themselves to hell in order to watch 15 minutes of a non-competitive game is simply not worth the sacrifice. Particularly when it can lead to dangerous health conditions. But to blame typical summer heat in Austin, Texas on climate change is absurd and ridiculous. Romero was quick to block anyone pointing that out to her, but the average high in Austin for this time of year is 95 to 97 degrees. It was a few degrees above that, but hardly out of the ordinary for that part of Texas in early September. Blaming climate change for it being hot in the summer in Texas is beyond ridiculous. And par for the course for modern sports editors and the LA Times. The entire climate change industrial complex has been repeatedly proven wrong, as Al Gore's "An Inconvenient Truth" inadvertently exposed. To Romero, though, it's part of an encoded set of religious beliefs that take precedence due to their association with modern liberalism. There is no doubting or questioning of "The Science" in her world, therefore a hot day in Austin must be an example of climate change. OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD Weather isn't climate, you see, until it's convenient. Again, Texas shouldn't be hosting a home game in the first week of September at two in the afternoon. That part's true. Blaming normal weather on climate change is blatantly false. No matter how many people telling the truth she blocks.

articles.title: ‘It’s madness’: Anand loses on time after declining draw against Sindarov; 20-year-old calls legend ‘world-class’
articles.summary: Chess News: BENGALURU: Viswanathan Anand’s difficult start to the 2026 Global Chess League took another turn for the worse on Tuesday as the five-time world champ.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Viswanathan Anand’s difficult start to the 2026 Global Chess League took another turn for the worse on Tuesday as the five-time world champion suffered two defeats in a day, the second coming in painful fashion against 20-year-old Javokhir Sindarov.Playing for Alaskan Knights, Anand had already endured a tough Monday, losing on time to World No. 1 Magnus Carlsen before holding Triveni Continental Kings’ Alireza Firouzja to a draw. Tuesday brought little relief. Anand first resigned against Ian Nepomniachtchi earlier in the day and then, in the evening, ran out of time against Sindarov despite having chances to win.The defeat was particularly frustrating because Anand, playing White, had held the advantage at one stage. With the clock becoming an increasingly important factor in this rapid format, however, the veteran struggled to keep control of the position.To make matters worse, Sindarov had offered a draw. Anand declined, believing he could still press for a win.“It’s just a comedy of errors. He offered a draw when he played 43...Re4+. But it seemed to me that his pieces had no coordination, so I tried to play for win,” Anand, visibly devastated after the loss on time, told reporters.“And then, it’s madness. I think even at the very end, I must have had a draw, but I went with 70.Kxd4+. I already blundered allowing 73.Rf8...Rc4+, and I can’t take on B4,” he explained.Asked what was going wrong for him, Anand could offer little explanation. “I don’t know. If I knew, I would do something,” he remarked.Sindarov, who is preparing to challenge for the world championship later this year, was hardly delighted with his own performance despite securing the crucial win.“Yeah, general happy with the performance but not happy with the game. But, I mean, in the opening, I played very well, but then, like, I made big mistake. I start thinking for five minutes to find the best moves, but in this time control, it’s always hard to find all the best moves,” he said.Sindarov confirmed that he had offered Anand a draw and admitted he was relieved when the Indian legend declined.“I saw the screen. I was just hoping, like, my draw will be, I mean, not so bad. But then I saw they’re just losing, and I was very happy when he didn’t accept my draw. And I was thinking, ‘Okay, I need to go all in, like, I will win or lose.’”With both players reduced to mere seconds, Sindarov felt Anand’s dwindling clock gave him a psychological edge.“I started to understand he felt a little bit nervous when his time was going to less than one minute, and then, somehow, I took this psychological advantage, and I started trying to push, and he missed my last trick,” he said.Despite beating Anand twice in two games, Sindarov played down any suggestion that he has a particular edge over the legend. "No. I mean, I’m just so lucky to win both games,” he added. “It’s very good to play against Anand always, getting, you know, practice against a world champion.”And when asked how highly he rated Anand at 56, Sindarov was full of praise: “He’s world-class," He said. "There are only a few players who can play at this level so close to 60 years old. So, that’s why he was one of the best.”What happened on Day 4 in Bengaluru The day started with Ganges Grandmasters beating Alaskan Knights 12-8. American Grandmaster Abhimanyu Mishra’s game against Leon Luke Mendonca ended in controversy after an illegal move and confusion over the clock cost Mishra a likely win.Mumba Masters defeated American Gambits 11-6 in the second match of the day. Triveni Continental Kings beat Pipers 10-4. The much-anticipated clash between Magnus Carlsen and Alireza Firouzja ended in a draw, but the Continental Kings picked up wins on other boards.Before the fourth edition began, Carlsen had joked that he wanted to “flag the s*** out of Alireza Firouzja”. articles.title: Are women better than men at endurance running?
articles.summary: Women have beaten men in some high-profile endurance events in recent months - are they better suited to these challenges?
articles.body:
"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."

Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.

Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.

Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.

But now, increasingly, she is not alone.

Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.

It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.

All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.

But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?

In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.

Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.

But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.

The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners

Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.

For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.

Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.

Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.

Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.

However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".

"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.

That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.

"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."

Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.

And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.

"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."

During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.

"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.

"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."

That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.

The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.

"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."

So can we explain why women might be more resilient?

Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.

"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."

McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".

"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.

"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."

One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.

Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.

Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.

Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.

And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.

"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."

The runner who went viral and sparked a campaign for change for women

Mashed potato & 19 minutes' sleep - Entrekin's epic race

When it comes to participation, visibility is key.

Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".

And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.

"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.

Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.

"When the proportion is so low, we have no clue what women are capable of. We're starting to see more women get faster and enter the sport and push themselves and break records. So, who knows where we'll be 10-15 years later down the line?"

New Orleans Pelicans center Derik Queen is looking to build on his impressive stint in his rookie year, which earned him a spot on the All-Rookie Second Team.

Queen displayed his all-around acumen at such a young age, even drawing comparisons to Denver Nuggets center Nikola Jokic . The 21-year-old pivot could see more opportunities in his sophomore season, as the Pelicans do not have many options for an interior presence.

A fan, however, was skeptical about Queen's possible ascent.

"The player I'm most nervous about long-term is Derik Queen . It has ZERO to do with his skill set. Something just seems off. Don't know what it is," wrote the fan on X.

Queen, who has an easygoing personality, dropped a glorious response .

"Does it have to do with me being fat and slow?" asked Queen, quite sarcastically.

His response has gone viral, garnering 1.2 million views as of this writing.

After Queen's comment, the fan heaped praise on the talented center, calling him an "elite basketball player" and "beloved in the state of Maryland."

The Pelicans selected Queen with the No. 13 pick in last year's NBA Draft after a one-and-done stint at Maryland. He averaged 11.7 points, 7.1 rebounds, 3.7 assists, and 1.0 steals in 81 games for New Orleans .

He recorded two triple-doubles, joining NBA legend Chris Paul as the only rookies in team history to register multiple triple-doubles.

Queen is slotted behind fellow center Yves Missi in the depth chart, but he has a clear path to take over in the starting unit if he continues his stellar play.

articles.summary: The Los Angeles Chargers released their first unofficial depth chart ahead of Week 1. Here are three things that stood out the most.
articles.body:
The Chargers reconstructed their coaching staff and roster this offseason. Now, it's time to take the field.

With five days until the Bolts' first game of the 2026 regular season, they released their unofficial depth chart going into Week 1 .

Oronde Gadsden II slides down the depth chart

At tight end, newly signed Charlie Kolar and David Njoku make up the starters, with Oronde Gadsden II listed as the third player at the position on the depth chart. As a rookie in 2025, the Syracuse product exploded onto the scene, catching 49 passes for 664 yards and three touchdowns. He rapidly became a trust target for quarterback Justin Herbert . The explanation for Gadsden's spot on the depth chart isn't a lack of talent, but rather a scheme adjustment as blocking is non-negotiable in Mike McDaniel's offense, which is an area where Kolar and Njoku have a leg up over Gadsden.

Del'Shawn Phillips starting with Denzel Perryman on IR

Denzel Perryman was placed on injured reserve, which broke open a vacancy at the starting linebacker spot alongside Daiyan Henley , which appears to be going to Phillips over Troy Dye and Marlowe Wax . In his first season with the Bolts, Phillips set a franchise single-season record with 24 special teams tackles, earning Second-Team All-Pro honors. It earned him a two-year, $7.5 million extension with the Chargers . While he has played primarily on special teams throughout his seven-year career, Phillips proved his capability on defense late last season while filling in. He finished with a career-high 37 tackles, a sack, and a fumble recovery.

Starter at left guard remains undetermined

The left guard designation listed a two-way tie: Kayode Awosika OR Trey Pipkins III. Rather than naming a definitive starter, the coaching staff is leaning toward a rotation. Head coach Jim Harbaugh said rookie Travis Burke's emergence as a swing tackle has made it possible that they play both Pipkins and Awosika. Harbaugh hinted at this unique approach, calling it "platooning" guards and "playing the hot hand."
